rewrites.summary:
The national framework governs recognition here, and the March 2026 amendment narrows it: both houses of parliament passed the amendment to the 2019 Transgender Persons Act that removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricts legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinner) and intersex people — excluding self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people — and requires medical certification for identity recognition, with medical boards and district authorities certifying gender-affirming surgery; human-rights reporting adds a new offence carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026. Recognition is already thin in practice: only about 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons — a small fraction — hold identity cards.

No Mizoram-specific trans statute or enforcement record is on file; neither international reporting on the change nor any other source on file records Mizoram-level deviation — statute, ban, or enforcement campaign — in either direction. The northeast state’s day-to-day exposure for a trans visitor therefore runs through the central framework, its pending narrowing included.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The change is not settled: the amendment drew nationwide protests from community groups and opposition parties, a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, and human-rights reporting warned the new coercion offence could criminalise support networks and urged the president not to sign, with presidential assent still pending as of late March 2026. The turbulence is national rather than division-specific — it belongs to the parent nation’s legislative process — and no neighbouring-division comparison appears in the record.
rewrites.localsOnly: Mizoram is one of the 12 states/UTs that have constituted the transgender welfare board under the 2020 national rules; an RTI investigation found most such boards are “rudderless” — without a policy framework, compliance mechanism or real power. All boards are resident-facing service bodies with no visitor-facing function.
